author: Bryanna Moore
title: Louisiana climbs in national education rankings, leaders calling it 'The Louisiana Leap' - NewsBreak
text:
By Bryanna Moore ,
6 hours ago
BATON ROUGE, La. (Louisiana First) — Louisiana education leaders are celebrating major gains in student performance after the state was recognized for some of the fastest academic improvement in the country.
State leaders say Louisiana ranked 49th in the nation for educational outcomes in 2019. Today, the state ranks 32nd for educational attainment, according to officials.
“The Nation’s Report Card” also ranked Louisiana No. 1 in the country for K-12 education improvement from 2022 to 2026.
Gov. Jeff Landry and State Superintendent of Education Cade Brumley called the progress part of what they describe as the “Louisiana Leap,” pointing to years of academic growth after the state once ranked near the bottom nationally.
“Today’s announcement marks the continuation of that truth for all of us,” Brumley said. “Further evidence of why other states north, south, east and west are calling on Louisiana as the exemplar for education.”
State leaders said poor rankings in 2019 became motivation to improve outcomes across Louisiana schools.
Brumley said while the state is encouraged by the latest results, officials acknowledge there is still more work to do.
“As I’ve said before, we are indeed pleased, but we’re not satisfied,” Brumley said.
Brumley noted that too many students are still not reading or performing math at grade level. He said the state continues working to improve academic achievement while also addressing chronic absenteeism and truancy.
He said officials are focused on helping schools and families identify attendance problems early so students can remain on track academically.
Landry also referenced Louisiana’s recent recognition at the national level during a visit to the White House.
“I was at an event over at the White House the other day, and they were giving us accolades on Louisiana being first,” Landry said. “I want you to know, he was a little shocked. I like it because I get to go back and tell him, ” Guess what? It’s not a shock. It’s a reality.”
